extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: scientists, practitioners, museum curators and instrument buyers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and standards for scientific books, museum catalogues, specimen collections, and laboratory apparatus as discussed in a Nature issue (book reviews, catalogue critique, and instrument/collection advertisements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and practical usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The book should present a clear account of general principles and be a mine of useful information, helpful alike to the practitioner and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works on clinical or applied topics must combine clear exposition of principles with abundant, usable information. The review praises the volume for presenting general principles clearly and being a work of reference useful to both practitioners and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of local detail with expert judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed local information must be combined with special experience and power of selection; in difficult or individual cases the expert should have the last word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guides should acknowledge limits of general advice and indicate when specialist/expert judgement is required. The review notes the vast amount of detailed locality information and stresses that the expert must, of course, have the last word in difficult individual cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of non-climatic environmental factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of health-resorts and climatic therapy should emphasise the influence of environment and travel per se, as often more essential elements of treatment than climate or baths alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should treat travel and broader environmental context (not only climate metrics) as therapeutic factors. The review commends the book for rightly emphasising these influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate, useful classification of climates
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctions between types of marine and other climates should be usefully drawn and provide practical recommendations (e.g., which climates suit which disorders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes useful distinctions (equable humid climates like Madeira vs relatively dry western Riviera; bracing northern seaside resorts) and values practical equivalences (elevation effects in Britain vs southern Europe). Such classificatory clarity is a criterion of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis and up-to-date empirical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should summarise recent additions to knowledge (e.g., soil and subsoil effects) and indicate where empirical observations remain to be collated and systematised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good treatises synthesise new empirical findings and identify gaps for future systematic work. The review praises the summary but calls for further collation/systematisation of empirical observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding of therapeutic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about therapeutic effects (e.g., of mineral waters) should be founded upon exact observation and evidence; minute quantities may have real importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer emphasises that balneotherapy has been refounded on exact observation and that even very dilute mineral constituents may be therapeutically important; authors should convey empirical bases rather than rely on tradition or imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical clinical guidance (selection, dosage, after-cure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical treatises must give clinicians clear guidance on selection and employment of baths, appropriate dosage/temperatures, duration of courses, and the necessity of an 'after-cure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and employment of baths belong mainly to the spa physician, but practical manuals should provide usable indications. The review warns failures arise from neglect of after-cure, too prolonged courses, or baths at too high temperature, and highlights under-emphasis on subthermal baths (below blood heat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear indications for climatic and spa treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Closing chapters (or summary sections) should give usable indications for when to choose climatic vs spa treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers who must select health-resorts require explicit guidance on indications; the review states the discussion of indications will be of service to those selecting resorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cataloguing should arrange specimens into species groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Museum catalogues should arrange specimens into groups of species (not merely list locality-numbered specimens) so the worker can express opinions about relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer criticises Mr. Bernard for abandoning the time-honoured plan of arranging specimens into species groups and instead ticketing each specimen by locality and a meaningless number. Good catalogues enable the author to express taxonomic opinions via arrangement into specific groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include author's interpretive synthesis and taxonomic opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Catalogues should contain more than bald statements of facts—description, tables and lists—by including the author's thoughts, opinions and systematic judgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review says Bernard's catalogues have descriptions and figures but 'not one word concerning the thoughts or opinions of the man' and likens them to a quantity surveyor's estimate without an architect's plan. Interpretive commentary is expected and valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of classification system should facilitate systematic work
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if difficult to apply, use of a system (e.g., Linnean) that enables expression of relationships and stimulates careful observation is preferable to purely descriptive inventories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer defends the Linnean system's advantage in enabling naturalists to arrange specimens into specific groups and thereby stimulate observation and systematic zoology, despite inherent difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate anatomical (soft-part) study with skeletal characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic studies should include soft-part anatomy of many specimens and compare anatomical characters with skeletal growth to distinguish intrinsic (heritable) traits from environmental ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review urges a 'systematic study of the soft parts' and a large-sample comparison to identify characters valuable for classification and to clear up intrinsic versus environmentally induced variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museum collections should be arranged systematically by curators
rubrics_metrics.description: Curators should not adopt a 'non possumus' attitude but should attempt to arrange their coral (and similar) collections in systematic groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer warns it would be a serious mistake for collection-holders to be content with Bernard's approach and recommends active attempts at systematic grouping to make collections useful for taxonomic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and report biogeographical and morphological differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Works on taxonomy/catalogues should note consistent regional differences (e.g., Atlantic vs Indo-Pacific skeletal differences) and consider their taxonomic importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer highlights an important observation: trabecular elements are thicker and coarser in Atlantic/West Indian forms than Indo-Pacific. Catalogues should record such patterns and suggest further investigation (including checking correspondence with anatomy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen selection and measurement by competent expert
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimen collections (e.g., crystal sets) should be carefully selected by a competent mineralogist and measured individually where necessary to ensure correct classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising text states crystals are 'carefully selected by a competent mineralogist' and 'have been measured individually wherever necessary' to insure correct classification; this is presented as a quality criterion for teaching collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear identification and documentation of specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Each specimen should be numbered and correspond to a printed list giving name and scientific description of the different forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification protocols: number specimens and supply a prepared printed list with names and scientific descriptions, facilitating student practice and correct use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality guarantee and return policy for institutional collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections should come with a clear quality guarantee (e.g., return within ten days at seller's expense and full refund) and assume risk of loss or breakage in transit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sample crystal set advertises a ten-day return/refund policy and liability for transport loss/breakage—presented as an assurance that institutions will be pleased; such service policies are part of collection-quality standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory apparatus: durability, accuracy, and suitability for teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical apparatus (the 'Technical' series) should be specially designed to stand hard work in school laboratories, produce accurate results, and offer good value compared with cheaper catalogue items of little service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers should prioritise robust construction and accuracy appropriate for educational labs; the review/advertisement contrasts useful, slightly costlier apparatus versus cheap items 'of practically no service.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruments should meet recognised tests and be certifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific instruments intended for observatories and schools should be able to pass recognised tests (e.g., Kew Observatory test) and be provided with certificates on request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adverts note instruments 'will pass the Kew Observatory test' and Kew certificates are available for a fee; meeting external standards and offering certification is a quality criterion for instruments.
